decks.title: Plant Growth and Development — Part 1: Growth, differentiation and development
goals: Describe the phases and conditions of growth
Distinguish arithmetic and geometric growth and read a sigmoid curve
Explain differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation and plasticity

slides.heading: Growth and development
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how plants grow, specialise and change form.

visual.alt: Flow from growth to differentiation to development

slides.narration: A seed becomes a seedling, then a flowering plant. Three processes take part: growth, which is an increase in size, differentiation, in which cells take up special roles, and development, which is the sum of all the changes in the life of the plant.

slides.heading: What is growth?
slides.body_md: **Growth** is a **permanent, irreversible increase in size** of an organ or cell, using energy. Plants show **indeterminate (open) growth** because **meristems** keep dividing at root and shoot tips throughout life.

visual.alt: Flow of the three phases of growth: meristematic, elongation and maturation

slides.narration: Growth is irreversible, so a cell that swells with water and then shrinks has not grown. Plants keep adding new organs because their meristems stay active throughout life. At a growing tip there are three phases: cells divide, then enlarge, and finally mature.

slides.heading: Measuring growth
slides.body_md: Growth can be measured by several **parameters**: cell number, length, area, volume, fresh weight and dry weight.

visual.alt: Table of parameters used to measure plant growth with an example of each

slides.narration: Different organs call for different measurements. A pollen tube is measured by its length, a leaf blade by its area, a fruit by its volume, and a root tip by the number of new cells it makes. Fresh weight and dry weight can be used for whole seedlings.

slides.heading: Arithmetic and geometric growth
slides.body_md: **Arithmetic:** only one daughter cell keeps dividing, so $L_t = L_0 + rt$, a straight line. **Geometric:** both daughters divide, so $W_t = W_0 e^{rt}$, an exponential curve.

slides.narration: In arithmetic growth, one daughter cell goes on dividing and the other matures, so length rises by the same amount in each unit of time. This is seen in a root elongating at a constant rate. In geometric growth, both daughter cells divide, so the size grows slowly at first and then very fast.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: arithmetic growth
slides.body_md: A root is 2 cm long and grows by 0.8 cm a day at a constant rate. Find its length after 6 days, and the time it takes to reach 11 cm.
bullets: The length-time graph is a straight line with slope 0.8 cm per day.

visual.alt: Worked table: 6.8 cm after 6 days

slides.narration: Use the equation for arithmetic growth. The starting length of two centimetres plus point eight centimetres a day for six days gives six point eight centimetres. To reach eleven centimetres, divide the gain of nine centimetres by the rate, which gives eleven and a quarter days.

slides.heading: Quick check: arithmetic growth
slides.body_md: Find the rate or length for a shoot growing arithmetically.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use length equals starting length plus rate times time.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: geometric growth
slides.body_md: A cell culture weighs 2 g and grows geometrically with a relative growth rate of 0.2 per day. Find its weight after 5 days. If cells double every 2 hours from a single cell, how many cells are there after 10 hours?
bullets: $W_t = W_0 e^{rt} = 2 \times e^{0.2 \times 5} = 2e \approx 5.44$ g.
Five doublings in 10 hours: $1 \times 2^{5} = 32$ cells.
Both results show growth that speeds up as there are more dividing cells.

visual.alt: Worked table: 5.44 g and 32 cells

slides.narration: Put the numbers into the exponential equation. Two grams times e to the power of one gives about five point four four grams. For the doubling culture, ten hours holds five doublings, and two to the power of five is thirty two cells.

slides.heading: The sigmoid growth curve
slides.body_md: Growth in a limited environment follows an **S-shaped** curve: a **lag phase** (slow), a **log or exponential phase** (fastest, geometric), and a **stationary phase** (growth levels off as resources run short or cells age).

slides.heading: Conditions for growth
slides.body_md: Growth needs **water**, **oxygen**, **nutrients**, a suitable **temperature**, and is affected by **light** and **gravity**.

rows: Cells need turgor to enlarge; also a medium for enzymes
Needed for aerobic respiration to release energy
Macro and micro nutrients for protoplasm and wall synthesis
Each plant grows best in a certain range
Affect growth and the direction of organs

visual.alt: Table of conditions needed for plant growth

slides.narration: Water gives turgor, so cells can enlarge. Oxygen supports respiration, which releases energy for growth. Nutrients supply the raw materials. Each plant has a range of temperature in which it grows best, and light and gravity influence the direction in which organs grow.

slides.heading: Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
slides.body_md: Cells from meristems **differentiate** into permanent cells with special structures. Permanent cells can **dedifferentiate**, regaining the power to divide (**callus**, interfascicular cambium), then **redifferentiate** to take up new roles.

visual.alt: Flow from a meristematic cell to a permanent cell, then dedifferentiation and redifferentiation

slides.narration: Differentiation is the process by which cells formed from the meristem become specialised, for example into a vessel with a lignified wall. Differentiated cells can revert to the dividing state, which is dedifferentiation, as happens when a wound heals. The new cells may then differentiate again, which is redifferentiation.

slides.heading: Plasticity and development
slides.body_md: **Plasticity** is the ability of a plant to form different structures in response to environment or phase of life: **heterophylly**, as in cotton, coriander and larkspur. **Development** is the sum of growth and differentiation over the whole life of the plant.

rows: Juvenile leaves differ in shape from mature leaves
Juvenile leaves differ in shape from mature leaves
Juvenile leaves differ in shape from mature leaves
Leaves in air differ from leaves in water

visual.alt: Table of heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur and buttercup

slides.narration: Some plants produce leaves of different shapes at different stages, or in different environments. This is heterophylly, a kind of plasticity, seen in cotton, coriander and larkspur. Development includes all the changes from seed to death: growth, differentiation, and the formation of flowers and fruits.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Growth: irreversible increase in size; plants have indeterminate growth through meristems.
Phases: meristematic, elongation, maturation.
Arithmetic growth: L equals L0 plus rt (linear). Geometric growth: W equals W0 e to the rt (exponential).
Sigmoid curve: lag, log, stationary phases.
Conditions: water, oxygen, nutrients, temperature, light, gravity.
Differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation; plasticity (heterophylly); development.

slides.heading: Auxins
slides.body_md: **Auxins** (IAA, IBA, NAA, and synthetic **2,4-D**) are made at the tips of roots and shoots. They help initiate **rooting in cuttings**, maintain **apical dominance**, prevent **fruit and leaf drop**, and the synthetic 2,4-D is used as a **weed killer** for dicots.

rows: Indole butyric acid (IBA), naphthalene acetic acid (NAA)

visual.alt: Table of the physiological effects of auxins

slides.narration: Auxins were the first plant growth regulators to be discovered. Rooting powders contain auxins, which help cuttings produce roots. The growing terminal bud suppresses the lateral buds by apical dominance. Spraying NAA keeps fruits and leaves from falling early, and the auxin 2,4-D kills broad leaved weeds without harming grasses such as wheat.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: preparing a rooting solution
slides.body_md: A nursery needs 500 mL of a rooting solution containing 20 mg of IBA per litre, and wants to spray 2,4-D at 1.5 litres per 100 square metres on a weedy plot of 1200 square metres. Find the mass of IBA and the volume of spray.
bullets: Mass of IBA: $20 \text{ mg per L} \times 0.5 \text{ L} = 10$ mg.
Spray: $\dfrac{1200}{100} \times 1.5 = 18$ litres.
Always dissolve the regulator first in a little solvent, then make up the volume.

visual.alt: Worked table: 10 mg IBA and 18 litres spray

slides.narration: Concentration times volume gives the mass. Twenty milligrams per litre in half a litre needs ten milligrams. For the plot, one thousand two hundred square metres is twelve lots of one hundred, and twelve times one point five litres is eighteen litres.

slides.heading: Gibberellins
slides.body_md: **Gibberellins** (GA3 and others) were found from the fungus *Gibberella fujikuroi*, which causes the **foolish seedling** disease of rice. They **elongate stems**, cause **bolting** and **speed malting**.

rows: Sugarcane yield rises; grape stalks lengthen
Beet, cabbage: internodes elongate before flowering
Fruits stay on the tree longer

visual.alt: Table of the physiological effects of gibberellins

slides.narration: Rice seedlings infected with the fungus grew abnormally tall, which led to the discovery of gibberellins. They make stems longer, as in sugarcane, and make rosette plants such as cabbage bolt before flowering. Brewers use them to speed up malting.

slides.heading: Cytokinins
slides.body_md: **Cytokinins** promote **cell division**. Kinetin was found in autoclaved herring sperm DNA, and **zeatin** in maize kernels and coconut milk. They help **lateral shoot growth** and **delay senescence**.

rows: Kinetin from DNA; zeatin from maize and coconut milk

visual.alt: Table of the physiological effects of cytokinins

slides.narration: Cytokinins act mainly where there is rapid cell division, such as in root tips and young fruits. They overcome apical dominance, so lateral buds grow. They also delay the ageing of leaves by drawing nutrients to them, so the leaves stay green longer.

slides.body_md: Predict the effect of a regulator on detached leaves.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which regulator keeps cut leaves green?

slides.heading: Ethylene
slides.body_md: **Ethylene** is a **gaseous** regulator. It **ripens fruit**, hastens **senescence** and **abscission**, promotes **female flowers** in cucumber, breaks **dormancy** of potato tubers and promotes **flowering** in pineapple and mango.

visual.alt: Table of the physiological effects of ethylene

slides.narration: Ethylene is made in large amounts in ripening fruit and in tissues under stress. Because it is a gas, one ripe fruit in a closed space can ripen others. Ethephon, a liquid, releases ethylene and is sprayed to ripen fruit and to hasten flowering in pineapple.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a seed germination test
slides.body_md: 50 seeds were put in each of three dishes: water only, gibberellin, and abscisic acid. After a week, 18, 36 and 6 had germinated. Find the germination percentage in each dish.
bullets: Control: $\dfrac{18}{50} \times 100 = 36$ percent.
Gibberellin: $\dfrac{36}{50} \times 100 = 72$ percent, twice the control.
Abscisic acid: $\dfrac{6}{50} \times 100 = 12$ percent, much lower.

visual.alt: Worked table: 36, 72 and 12 percent

slides.narration: Divide the number germinated by fifty and multiply by one hundred. Water alone gives thirty six percent, gibberellin gives seventy two percent, which is double, and abscisic acid gives only twelve percent. The result shows that gibberellin promotes and abscisic acid inhibits germination.

slides.heading: Abscisic acid
slides.body_md: **Abscisic acid (ABA)** is the **stress hormone**. It **closes stomata**, induces **seed dormancy**, inhibits **seed germination**, promotes abscission and senescence, and acts as an **antagonist** of gibberellins.

visual.alt: Table of the physiological effects of abscisic acid

slides.narration: During drought, abscisic acid builds up and makes the stomata close, which saves water. It keeps seeds dormant until conditions improve, working against gibberellins, which promote germination.

slides.heading: Quick check: abscisic acid
slides.body_md: Match the response to the regulator.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which regulator closes stomata in a drought?

slides.heading: Working together or against
slides.body_md: Growth regulators seldom act alone. They may be **synergistic** or **antagonistic**.

rows: Auxin keeps lateral buds suppressed; cytokinin counters it
Gibberellin breaks dormancy and promotes germination; ABA maintains it

visual.alt: Table of interactions between plant growth regulators

slides.narration: Regulators often act together. Auxin suppresses lateral buds and cytokinin overcomes this. Gibberellin breaks dormancy and promotes germination, while abscisic acid keeps the seed dormant. A balance between them decides what the plant does.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Auxins: rooting, apical dominance, preventing drop, parthenocarpy, 2,4-D weed killer.
Gibberellins: stem elongation, bolting, malting.
Cytokinins: cell division, lateral shoots, delay senescence.
Ethylene: gas; ripening, senescence, abscission, female flowers.
Abscisic acid: stress hormone; stomatal closure, dormancy; antagonist of gibberellins.

rows: Cell division, enlargement, flowering, fruiting, seed formation
Ripening and senescence; can promote or inhibit

visual.alt: Table classifying plant growth regulators as promoters and inhibitors

slides.narration: To recap: auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins are promoters, abscisic acid is an inhibitor, and ethylene is a gas that can act either way. Each regulator has several effects, and they interact to control growth, dormancy and ageing.

notes.title: Plant Growth and Development — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Growth, differentiation and development
sections.body_md:
**Growth** is a **permanent, irreversible increase in size** of an organ, or even of a cell, accompanied by metabolic processes that use energy. Plants show **indeterminate (open) growth**: **meristems** at the root and shoot tips divide throughout life (**primary growth**), so new organs are formed continually. The meristematic cells of a growing region pass through three phases: the **meristematic phase** (cells divide), the **elongation phase** (cells enlarge, taking in water) and the **maturation phase** (cells differentiate into permanent cells).

Growth may be measured by an increase in **cell number**, **length**, **area**, **volume**, **fresh weight** or **dry weight**.

**Growth rate.** The increase in growth per unit time is the growth rate. In **arithmetic growth**, only one daughter cell of each division keeps dividing while the other differentiates and matures; the length increases linearly, $L_t = L_0 + rt$, where $L_t$ is the length at time $t$, $L_0$ at the start and $r$ the growth rate. In **geometric growth** both daughter cells keep dividing, so the growth is slow at first (lag phase) and then very fast (log or exponential phase), $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$, where $r$ is the **relative growth rate** and $e$ the base of natural logarithms. A plot of growth against time in a limited environment is a **sigmoid (S-shaped) curve**: a **lag phase**, a **log (exponential) phase** and a **stationary phase**, when growth slows as nutrients or space become limiting or as cells age. The **relative growth rate** compares growth with the initial size.

**Conditions for growth:** **water** (turgidity for enlargement; medium for enzymes), **oxygen** (energy from respiration), **nutrients** (macro- and micro-elements), a suitable **temperature**, and **light and gravity**.

**Differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation.** Cells derived from root and shoot apical meristems and from cambium differentiate and mature to perform specific functions; a vessel element, for example, develops a lignified secondary wall and loses its protoplasm. Living differentiated cells that have lost the capacity to divide can regain it under certain conditions: this is **dedifferentiation**, as in the formation of a **callus** or the interfascicular cambium. The cells produced may again lose the capacity to divide and mature: **redifferentiation**.

**Plasticity** is the ability of plants to follow different pathways in response to the environment or the phase of life, to form different kinds of structures. **Heterophylly** is an example: the leaves of the juvenile plant differ in shape from those of the mature plant in **cotton, coriander and larkspur**, and the leaves of **buttercup** produced in air and in water differ.

**Development** is the sum of all the changes that an organism goes through during its life, from germination to senescence, and includes growth and differentiation. It is under the control of intrinsic factors (genetic and chemical, including plant growth regulators) and extrinsic factors (light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition).

sections.heading: 2. Plant growth regulators
sections.body_md:
**Plant growth regulators (PGRs)** are small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition that control growth and development. They may be **promoters** (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins) or **inhibitors** (abscisic acid); ethylene can act as either.

**Auxins** (Greek *auxein*, to grow) include indole-3-acetic acid (**IAA**), indole butyric acid (**IBA**), naphthalene acetic acid (**NAA**) and the synthetic **2,4-D**. They are made at the tips of roots and shoots. The discovery began with the **Darwins**, who observed that the **tip of the coleoptile** perceives light and a signal moves down to make it bend towards the light; **Went** collected a substance from coleoptile tips in **agar blocks** and showed that a block placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile made it bend. Auxins help to **initiate rooting in stem cuttings**, promote **flowering** in pineapple, **prevent fruit and leaf drop** at early stages (and promote abscission of older leaves and fruits), maintain **apical dominance** (the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of lateral buds, so removing it, as in tea plantations and hedge-making, makes the plant bushy), induce **parthenocarpy** in tomato, control **xylem differentiation** and help in cell division. **2,4-D** is used to kill **dicotyledonous weeds**.

**Gibberellins** (GA3 is the best known) were discovered from the fungus *Gibberella fujikuroi*, which causes the **foolish seedling** disease of rice. They promote **elongation of stems** (increasing the length of grape stalks and of sugarcane stems, with higher sugar yield), improve the **shape and size of fruits** such as apple, **delay senescence** so that fruits stay on the tree longer, **speed up malting** in the brewing industry, and cause **bolting** (internode elongation before flowering) in beet, cabbage and other rosette plants.

**Cytokinins** promote **cell division** (cytokinesis). **Kinetin** was found in autoclaved herring sperm DNA; **zeatin** was isolated from maize kernels and coconut milk. They help to produce **new leaves, lateral shoots and adventitious shoots**, overcome **apical dominance**, and **delay senescence** of leaves by promoting the mobilisation of nutrients to them. They are made where rapid cell division occurs, such as root apices, shoot buds and young fruits.

**Ethylene** is a **gaseous** regulator formed in large amounts in ripening fruits and in tissues undergoing senescence. It **hastens ripening** of fruits such as tomato and apple, **senescence and abscission** of leaves and flowers, promotes **female flowers** in cucumber, breaks **dormancy** of seeds and buds (potato tubers), initiates **rooting**, promotes **flowering** in pineapple and mango and causes **rapid internode and petiole elongation** in deepwater rice. **Ethephon** is the commonest source in agriculture.

**Abscisic acid (ABA)** is a **growth inhibitor**, called the **stress hormone**. It **inhibits seed germination**, induces **seed dormancy**, stimulates the **closure of stomata** and increases tolerance to stress, promotes abscission and senescence, and acts as an **antagonist** to gibberellic acid. Regulators work together or against each other, and the balance (not one alone) controls dormancy, flowering and ageing. (Photoperiodism and vernalisation are not part of this syllabus.)

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining growth as any change in size (it must be permanent and irreversible: a cell swelling with water and shrinking again has not grown).
- Placing the fastest growth in the lag or stationary phase (it is the log phase).
- Writing that cytokinins close stomata or that ABA promotes cell division (ABA is the stress hormone; cytokinins promote division).
- Saying ethylene is a liquid or a solid (it is a gas; ethephon is the liquid source).
- Mixing up dedifferentiation (regaining division, as in callus) with differentiation (specialisation).
- Using 2,4-D to kill monocot weeds (it kills dicot weeds).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a regulator and one effect; a growth phase; a definition term.
- 2–3-mark answers: arithmetic versus geometric growth; phases of the sigmoid curve; differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation; effects of one regulator.
- 5-mark answers: growth and its measurement with curve; plant growth regulators with discovery and uses.
- Numericals: growth rates, doubling, hormone solutions, germination percentages — write the equation first and show each step.

questions.stem_md: A dry bean seed, soaked for hours, swells to twice its size, and shrinks again when dried. Why is this swelling not counted as growth?

options.text_md: The increase takes place without any water being absorbed.
Growth occurs only in animals, which have determinate form.
Growth is counted only when cells decrease in number.
The increase in size is reversible, whereas growth is permanent and irreversible.

questions.solution_md: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size; a seed that swells with water and shrinks on drying has not grown — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A banyan tree that is hundreds of years old still puts out new branches and leaves every year, while a human stops adding new height in adult life. This is because in plants

options.text_md: all the cells of the plant keep dividing equally at all times
meristems are lost after the seedling stage, but cells enlarge for ever
meristems at the tips keep dividing throughout life, giving open growth
growth stops after flowering and later shoots are only repairs

questions.solution_md: Plants have indeterminate (open) growth because meristems at root and shoot tips retain the capacity to divide — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Under the microscope, cells about 4 mm behind a root tip are much longer than those at the tip, with large vacuoles, and are not dividing. These cells are in the

options.text_md: meristematic phase of growth
maturation phase of growth
elongation phase of growth
stationary phase of the growth curve

questions.solution_md: Cells that have stopped dividing and are enlarging, with large vacuoles, are in the elongation phase — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student plots the length of a bamboo shoot against time and gets a straight line. This suggests that

options.text_md: both daughter cells keep dividing, giving geometric growth
only one daughter cell of each division keeps dividing, giving arithmetic growth
no cell divides, so the growth is reversible
the shoot has reached the stationary phase of an S-shaped curve

questions.solution_md: A straight line of length against time is arithmetic growth: one daughter cell keeps dividing and the other differentiates — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A culture of plant cells shows a graph of cell number that rises slowly for a few days and then climbs very steeply. This pattern is typical of

options.text_md: arithmetic growth, in which only one daughter cell keeps dividing
determinate growth, in which cells never divide again
geometric growth, in which both daughter cells keep dividing
dedifferentiation, in which cells stop dividing for ever

questions.solution_md: Slow growth followed by a rapid exponential rise is geometric growth — option (c).

questions.stem_md: On the S-shaped growth curve of a seedling, the initial period of slow growth is called the

options.text_md: log phase
stationary phase
lag phase
maturation phase

questions.solution_md: The slow beginning of the sigmoid curve is the lag phase; the steep part is the log phase and the flat end is the stationary phase — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A seedling is measured every five days. Between which part of its sigmoid growth curve does it add the greatest height per day?

options.text_md: The lag phase at the start
The log (exponential) phase
The stationary phase at the end
The phase just after the seed is shed

questions.solution_md: Growth is fastest in the log or exponential phase, the steep middle of the S-curve — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A seedling in a small pot grows well for weeks, but then its height curve goes flat although it is still alive. The most likely reason is that

options.text_md: nutrients and space have become limiting, so growth enters the stationary phase
the meristem has begun a fresh exponential phase
dedifferentiation has made the leaves lose all their cells
arithmetic growth always stops when a plant is watered

questions.solution_md: In a limited environment growth levels off in the stationary phase as nutrients or space become limiting — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Maize seedlings grown in a pot that has been flooded for days grow very poorly, and their roots look weak. The most likely limiting factor for their growth is

options.text_md: oxygen, needed for respiration to release energy
carbon dioxide in the soil water
excess of light reaching the roots
lack of gravity acting on the pot

questions.solution_md: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen; roots need oxygen for aerobic respiration, which supplies energy for growth — option (a).

questions.stem_md: When the surface of a potato tuber is cut, mature parenchyma cells near the wound start dividing again and form a mass of cells called a callus. This process is

options.text_md: redifferentiation
dedifferentiation
differentiation of the meristem
senescence

questions.solution_md: Living differentiated cells regaining the capacity to divide is dedifferentiation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Some cells of a callus later lose the ability to divide and develop lignified walls to become vessel elements. This step is

options.text_md: dedifferentiation
plasticity of the juvenile leaf
the lag phase of growth
redifferentiation

questions.solution_md: Cells produced by dedifferentiation that lose division again and mature are redifferentiated — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A water buttercup produces feathery leaves under water and broad leaves in air. This ability to form different structures in different environments is called

options.text_md: dedifferentiation, shown here as callus formation
bolting, shown here as internode elongation
apical dominance, shown here as bud suppression
plasticity, shown here as heterophylly

questions.solution_md: Different leaf forms in air and water are heterophylly, an example of plasticity — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Seedling P grows from 2 cm to 4 cm and seedling Q from 10 cm to 14 cm in the same time. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: P gained more in length, and also has the higher relative growth rate.
Q gained more in length, and also has the higher relative growth rate.
Both have the same relative growth rate, because both grew.
Q gained more in length, but P has the higher relative growth rate.

questions.solution_md: Q gained 4 cm and P only 2 cm, but relative to the starting size P grew by 100 percent and Q by 40 percent — option (d).

False

options.text_md: True

A callus weighs 10 g and grows geometrically with a relative growth rate of 0.3 per day. What is its weight after 3 days, in g, to one decimal place? (Use e to the power 0.9 equal to 2.46.)
questions.solution_md: $W_t = W_0 e^{rt} = 10 \times e^{0.3 \times 3} = 10 \times 2.46 \approx 24.6$ g.

questions.solution_md: Growth $= 12 - 6 = 6$ cm in 5 days, so the rate is $\dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2$ cm per day.

questions.stem_md: Define growth. Why is plant growth described as indeterminate?

answer.model_answer_md: **Growth** is a **permanent, irreversible increase in size** of an organ or even of a cell, accompanied by metabolic processes that use energy. Plant growth is **indeterminate (open)** because **meristems** at the root and shoot tips keep **dividing throughout life**, so new organs are formed continually.

questions.solution_md: Definition and open growth.

questions.stem_md: Name the three phases of growth in a region of a growing root, and state what happens to the cells in each.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **meristematic phase** the cells **divide**. In the **elongation phase** they **enlarge**, taking up water and forming large vacuoles, which lengthens the root. In the **maturation phase** they **differentiate** into the specialised cells of permanent tissues.

questions.solution_md: Meristematic, elongation, maturation.

questions.stem_md: Explain dedifferentiation and redifferentiation, with one example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dedifferentiation** is the regaining of the capacity to divide by living, differentiated cells, as when mature cells at a wound form a **callus**. The cells produced may again lose the capacity to divide and **mature**: this is **redifferentiation**, for example callus cells becoming xylem vessels.

questions.solution_md: Definitions with callus example.

questions.stem_md: Why do seeds sown in dry, compacted and waterlogged soils both grow poorly? Link each case to the conditions needed for growth.

answer.model_answer_md: Growth needs **water**, **oxygen** and **nutrients**. In **dry** soil there is too little water for cells to gain **turgor** and enlarge. In **compacted or waterlogged** soil there is too little **oxygen** for aerobic respiration, which supplies energy. Suitable temperature and nutrients are also needed.

questions.solution_md: Water for turgor; oxygen for respiration.

marking_scheme.step: Waterlogged or compacted soil: oxygen and respiration

questions.stem_md: Distinguish arithmetic growth from geometric growth, giving the equation for each.

answer.model_answer_md: In **arithmetic growth** only **one daughter cell** keeps dividing while the other matures, so length increases linearly, $L_t = L_0 + rt$, and the graph is a **straight line**. In **geometric growth** **both** daughter cells keep dividing, so size increases exponentially, $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$, where $r$ is the relative growth rate, and the graph is a **curve** that is slow at first and then very fast.

questions.solution_md: Division pattern, graph, equation.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three phases of the sigmoid growth curve of a plant and say why growth slows in the last phase.

answer.model_answer_md: The **lag phase** is the slow start of growth. In the **log (exponential) phase** growth is **fastest**, as in geometric growth. In the **stationary phase** growth **slows** and levels off, because **nutrients or space become limiting**, or because cells **age**. The whole curve is **S-shaped**.

questions.solution_md: Lag, log, stationary phases; why growth slows.

questions.stem_md: What is plasticity in plants? Explain it with heterophylly, giving two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: **Plasticity** is the ability of plants to follow **different pathways** and form **different structures** in response to the environment or the phase of life. In **heterophylly** the leaves of the **juvenile** plant differ in shape from those of the **mature** plant, as in **cotton, coriander and larkspur**; the leaves of **buttercup** formed in air differ from those formed in water.

questions.solution_md: Plasticity defined; heterophylly examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the phases and the measurement of growth in plants, compare arithmetic and geometric growth, and name the conditions necessary for growth.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Phases.** Cells at a growing region pass through the **meristematic** phase (division), the **elongation** phase (enlargement) and the **maturation** phase (differentiation). Meristems keep dividing, so growth is open.

**Measurement.** Growth is measured by increase in cell number, length, area, volume, fresh weight or dry weight, as suits the organ.

**Rates.** In **arithmetic** growth one daughter cell keeps dividing and length increases linearly, $L_t = L_0 + rt$. In **geometric** growth both keep dividing and size increases exponentially, $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$. In a limited environment the curve is **S-shaped** with lag, log and stationary phases.

**Conditions.** Water, oxygen, nutrients and a suitable temperature, with light and gravity influencing growth.

questions.solution_md: Phases, measurement, rates, conditions.

questions.stem_md: A seedling's height (cm) was recorded at days 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 as 2, 3, 6, 12, 22, 30, 34, 35. Work out the growth in each interval and the fastest growth rate, identify the three phases, and explain what the pattern shows about the way the seedling grows.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Increments** in the seven five-day intervals: 1, 3, 6, 10, 8, 4 and 1 cm. The **fastest** growth is between days 15 and 20: 10 cm in 5 days, a rate of 2 cm per day.

**Phases.** Days 0 to 10, with growth rates of only 0.2 and 0.6 cm per day, form the **lag phase**; days 10 to 25 are the **log phase**, with the steepest rise; after day 25 growth falls to 0.8 and then 0.2 cm per day: the **stationary phase**.

**Meaning.** Growth is slow, then exponential, then limited: an **S-shaped (sigmoid) curve**, typical of growth in a limited environment as nutrients or space become limiting.

questions.solution_md: Increments, fastest rate, phases and meaning.

questions.stem_md: Explain differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation with the example of a wounded tissue, and describe plasticity and development.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Differentiation.** Cells from the root and shoot apical meristems and from cambium mature and take up specific functions; a vessel element, for example, develops a lignified wall and loses its protoplasm.

**Dedifferentiation.** Living differentiated cells that have lost the capacity to divide can regain it, as when mature cells at a wound divide to form a **callus**.

**Redifferentiation.** The cells produced may again lose the capacity to divide and mature into specialised cells, for example xylem.

**Plasticity.** Plants can form different structures in response to the environment or phase of life, as in **heterophylly** of cotton, coriander, larkspur and buttercup.

**Development.** It is the sum of growth and differentiation during the whole life of the plant, controlled by intrinsic factors, including growth regulators, and extrinsic factors such as light, temperature, water, oxygen and nutrients.

questions.solution_md: Three processes, plasticity and development.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: A student cuts a thin slice from the middle of a carrot root and places it on a nutrient medium. After some days the cut surface shows a white mass of dividing cells, which started from 5 cells and went through 4 rounds of division, each cell dividing once in every round. A few weeks later, some cells in the mass develop lignified walls and form tubes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) dedifferentiation

**(b)** 80

**(c)** (i) The process is **redifferentiation**: cells formed by dedifferentiation lose the capacity to divide and **mature** into specialised cells, here **xylem vessels**. This shows that the cells of the callus can again take up **specific functions**.

**OR** (ii) It is **geometric**, because **every cell divides** in each round, so the number doubles each time: 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 cells. In arithmetic growth only one daughter cell would continue dividing.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Mature, living cells regaining the capacity to divide, forming a callus, is dedifferentiation — option (d).

**(b)** $5 \times 2^{4} = 80$ cells.

**(c)** (i) Redifferentiation to vessels.

(ii) Geometric; doubling.

children.stem_md: The formation of the white mass of dividing cells from mature cells is

options.text_md: redifferentiation
senescence
the stationary phase
dedifferentiation

children.solution_md: Mature, living cells regaining the capacity to divide, forming a callus, is dedifferentiation — option (d).

children.stem_md: How many cells are in the mass after the 4 rounds of division?
**Either** (i): Name the process by which some cells develop lignified walls and form tubes, and say what this shows about the cells of the mass.

answer.model_answer_md: The process is **redifferentiation**: cells formed by dedifferentiation lose the capacity to divide and **mature** into specialised cells, here **xylem vessels**. This shows that the cells of the callus can again take up **specific functions**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Is the growth of the white mass arithmetic or geometric? Give a reason from the data.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **geometric**, because **every cell divides** in each round, so the number doubles each time: 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 cells. In arithmetic growth only one daughter cell would continue dividing.

questions.stem_md: Oat coleoptiles are lit from one side. One with its tip covered by an opaque cap does not bend; another with the cap fixed over its base, tip left exposed, bends towards the light. What do the two results show together?

options.text_md: The tip perceives the light, and a signal then moves down to the growing region.
The base perceives the light and sends a signal up to the tip.
Light is not needed for bending, because the cap makes no difference.
Only the cap material, and not the plant, decides the bending.

questions.solution_md: Covering the tip stops the bending but covering the base does not, so the tip perceives light and a signal passes down — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An agar block that had stood under coleoptile tips in the dark is placed on one side of the cut top of a decapitated coleoptile. After some hours the coleoptile bends away from the side bearing the block. This showed that

options.text_md: agar itself is a growth regulator that stops growth on its side
light from the lamp, and not the tip, causes the bending
the coleoptile bends only if it still has its own tip
a chemical substance from the tip, later named auxin, makes the cells on that side grow faster

questions.solution_md: The block carried a diffusible growth-promoting substance, auxin, which made the cells below it elongate more, so the coleoptile bent away — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A nursery owner dips the cut ends of rose stem cuttings in a powder before planting them, to make them form roots quickly. The powder most probably contains

options.text_md: abscisic acid, the stress hormone
an auxin such as IBA or NAA
ethylene, a gaseous ripening regulator
a cytokinin that stops root growth

questions.solution_md: Auxins such as IBA and NAA help initiate rooting in stem cuttings — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gardener pinches off the tip of a young tea shoot, and soon several side branches grow from the buds below. This is explained by the removal of

options.text_md: ethylene from the apical bud, which was ripening the lateral buds
abscisic acid from the lateral buds, which kept the apical bud dormant
gibberellin from the roots, which was stunting the lateral buds
auxin from the apical bud, which was suppressing the lateral buds

questions.solution_md: In apical dominance the apical bud, through auxin, suppresses lateral buds; removing it frees them to grow — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A farmer sprays a wheat field with 2,4-D, and the broad-leaved weeds die but the wheat survives. 2,4-D is

options.text_md: a synthetic auxin that kills monocotyledonous crops
a natural cytokinin from coconut milk
a synthetic auxin that kills dicotyledonous weeds
a gaseous regulator that ripens fruit

questions.solution_md: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin used as a weed killer for dicot weeds; monocots such as wheat are not harmed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Rice seedlings in a nursery bed grew abnormally tall and thin after a fungal infection, and later fell over. The regulators discovered from the fungus responsible are

options.text_md: cytokinins
abscisic acid
ethylene
gibberellins

questions.solution_md: The fungus Gibberella fujikuroi causes the foolish seedling disease of rice; gibberellins were first found from it — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A brewery wants to speed up the conversion of barley grains into malt. Which regulator would it spray?

options.text_md: Abscisic acid
Ethylene
Gibberellin

questions.solution_md: Gibberellins speed up malting in the brewing industry — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Detached leaves of a vegetable are kept in two jars: in one the cut stalks stand in plain water, in the other in a dilute solution of a regulator. The leaves in the second jar stay green much longer. The regulator is most likely a

options.text_md: abscisic acid, which delays senescence
cytokinin, which hastens senescence
cytokinin, which delays senescence
ethylene, which delays senescence

questions.solution_md: Cytokinins delay the senescence of leaves by promoting the mobilisation of nutrients to them — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A tissue culture technician adds a cytokinin to a medium and sees many shoots forming from the sides of a stem piece. This is mainly because cytokinins

options.text_md: close the stomata and raise stress tolerance
promote cell division and the growth of lateral shoots
hasten the ripening of the cut tissue
inhibit seed germination

questions.solution_md: Cytokinins promote cell division and lateral and adventitious shoot growth — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A shopkeeper stores raw bananas in a closed box with one ripe banana, and the raw ones ripen within days. The most likely cause is the gas

options.text_md: carbon dioxide given off by the box
ethylene given off by the ripe fruit
abscisic acid given off by the box
auxin given off by the raw bananas

questions.solution_md: Ethylene is a gaseous regulator that hastens fruit ripening, and a ripe fruit releases it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which plant growth regulator is a gas?

options.text_md: Ethylene
Auxin
Gibberellin
Cytokinin

questions.solution_md: Ethylene is the gaseous regulator — option (a).

questions.stem_md: During a long drought the leaves of a shrub lose water slowly because their stomata close. The hormone mainly responsible is

options.text_md: abscisic acid, the stress hormone
gibberellin, the stem-elongation hormone
kinetin, the cell-division hormone
IBA, the rooting hormone

questions.solution_md: Abscisic acid stimulates stomatal closure and increases tolerance to stress — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A seed will not germinate even in warm, moist soil, but starts to when soaked in a regulator solution. The seed was dormant under the influence of one regulator, and the soaking solution probably contained its antagonist. They are respectively

options.text_md: gibberellin and abscisic acid
abscisic acid and gibberellin
ethylene and auxin
cytokinin and abscisic acid

questions.solution_md: Abscisic acid induces dormancy and inhibits germination; gibberellin is its antagonist and breaks dormancy — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the lettered diagram, which panel shows the experiment in which an agar block that had stood under coleoptile tips is placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile in the dark?

options.text_md: Panel C
Panel A
Panel B
Panel E

questions.solution_md: The agar block experiment, showing a chemical from the tips, is panel C — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Removing the apical bud of a hedge plant makes it bushier.

**Reason (R):** The apical bud supplies auxin that suppresses the growth of lateral buds.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and removing the source of auxin releases the lateral buds, which explains the bushier growth — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ethylene is useful for ripening fruit in a closed store room.

**Reason (R):** Ethylene is a gaseous plant growth regulator.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but being a gas does not by itself explain why it ripens fruit; ripening is a specific effect of ethylene — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Abscisic acid promotes the germination of seeds.

**Reason (R):** Abscisic acid acts as an antagonist of gibberellins.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: abscisic acid inhibits germination and induces dormancy. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cytokinins promote the growth of lateral shoots.

**Reason (R):** Cytokinins are formed mainly in the fully mature leaf blades of a plant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: cytokinins are formed where rapid cell division occurs, such as root apices, shoot buds and young fruits — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Went’s agar block experiment showed that a chemical substance made at the coleoptile tip can cause bending.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. A block that had stood under tips made a decapitated coleoptile bend; the substance was auxin.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Ethylene delays the ripening of fruits and the senescence of leaves.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Ethylene hastens fruit ripening and the senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers.

questions.stem_md: The synthetic auxin sprayed to kill dicot weeds in a cereal field is ______.
Match each plant growth regulator (column I) with an effect (column II).

options.text_md: Auxin
Gibberellin
Cytokinin
Abscisic acid

questions.solution_md: Auxin initiates rooting; gibberellin elongates stems; cytokinin delays senescence; abscisic acid closes stomata.

questions.stem_md: A gardener needs 2.5 litres of a gibberellin solution of 100 mg per litre. How many mg of gibberellin must be dissolved?
questions.solution_md: Mass = concentration $\times$ volume $= 100 \times 2.5 = 250$ mg.

questions.stem_md: Name two uses of auxins in agriculture and horticulture, with a regulator or example for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Auxins such as **IBA and NAA** help **initiate rooting in stem cuttings**, so cuttings are dipped in them before planting. Auxins also **prevent early fruit and leaf drop**, for example **NAA** in orchards, and the synthetic auxin **2,4-D** is used as a **weed killer** for dicot weeds.

questions.solution_md: Two uses with examples.

questions.stem_md: State two effects of gibberellins that make them useful to a sugarcane farmer and to a brewer.

answer.model_answer_md: Gibberellins **elongate the stems** of sugarcane, so spraying increases stem length and **yield**. In the brewing industry they **speed up malting** of barley. They also cause bolting in rosette plants and improve the size and shape of fruits such as apple.

questions.solution_md: Sugarcane stem elongation; malting.

questions.stem_md: What are cytokinins? Name one natural source and two physiological effects.

answer.model_answer_md: Cytokinins are growth regulators that promote **cell division** (cytokinesis). A natural cytokinin, **zeatin**, was isolated from **maize kernels and coconut milk**; kinetin came from autoclaved herring sperm DNA. They promote **lateral shoot growth** and **delay leaf senescence**.

questions.solution_md: Cell division; source; two effects.

questions.stem_md: Why can a ripe fruit kept with unripe ones hasten their ripening? Name two other effects of the regulator concerned.

answer.model_answer_md: The ripe fruit gives off **ethylene**, a **gaseous** regulator that **hastens fruit ripening**; the gas reaches the neighbouring fruits. Ethylene also promotes **senescence and abscission** of leaves and flowers, and **female flowers** in cucumber.

questions.solution_md: Ethylene is a gas; two other effects.

questions.stem_md: Why is abscisic acid called the stress hormone? State two of its effects.

answer.model_answer_md: Abscisic acid builds up under stress such as drought. It stimulates the **closure of stomata**, which saves water, and **increases tolerance** to stress. It also induces **seed dormancy**, inhibits germination and promotes abscission and senescence; it is an **antagonist of gibberellins**.

questions.solution_md: Stress; stomatal closure; dormancy.

marking_scheme.step: Builds up under stress; stomatal closure

questions.stem_md: A tea planter plucks the tips of shoots regularly. Explain, using apical dominance and the role of cytokinins, why the bush becomes dense.

answer.model_answer_md: In **apical dominance** the growing **apical bud** suppresses the **lateral buds** through **auxin**. Plucking the tips removes this source of auxin, so the **lateral buds grow** and the bush becomes dense. **Cytokinins**, which promote cell division and lateral shoot growth, help to **overcome apical dominance**, as when applied to lateral buds.

questions.solution_md: Auxin from apical bud suppresses laterals; removal; cytokinin.

questions.stem_md: Describe the experiment by which Went showed that a chemical substance, and not light alone, causes the bending of a coleoptile.

answer.model_answer_md: Went cut off the **tips** of oat coleoptiles and placed them on **agar blocks**, so that a substance moved into the agar. He then put such a block **on one side of the cut top of a decapitated coleoptile**, in the **dark**. The coleoptile **bent away** from the side with the block, showing that a **chemical substance**, later named **auxin**, made the cells grow faster on that side.

questions.solution_md: Agar block experiment and conclusion.

questions.stem_md: Explain how gibberellins and abscisic acid act against each other in the life of a seed, and how auxin and cytokinin act against each other in a shoot.

answer.model_answer_md: **Abscisic acid** induces **seed dormancy** and inhibits germination; **gibberellins** break dormancy and promote germination, so they are **antagonists**, and the balance decides when the seed germinates. In a shoot, **auxin** from the apical bud **suppresses lateral buds**, while **cytokinins** promote lateral shoot growth and so **overcome apical dominance**.

questions.solution_md: GA versus ABA; auxin versus cytokinin.

questions.stem_md: An orchard owner wants fruits to stay on the trees longer, wants new cuttings to root, and wants to control broad-leaved weeds. Name the type of regulator for each purpose, with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: To **prevent early fruit drop** she can spray an **auxin such as NAA**. To make cuttings **root**, she can dip them in an **auxin such as IBA**. For **broad-leaved (dicot) weeds** she can spray the synthetic auxin **2,4-D**, which kills dicots but not grasses. All three purposes use auxins.

questions.solution_md: NAA, IBA, 2,4-D.

questions.stem_md: Describe the discovery of auxin from the experiments on coleoptiles, and list the physiological effects of auxins with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Discovery.** Charles and Francis Darwin observed that a coleoptile lit from one side bends towards the light, but not if its **tip** is covered or cut off, so the **tip perceives light** and a signal moves down. **Went** placed coleoptile tips on **agar blocks** and then put a block on one side of a decapitated coleoptile in the dark; it bent away from that side, showing that a **chemical substance, auxin**, caused the growth.

**Effects.** Auxins (IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D) **initiate rooting** in stem cuttings, promote flowering in pineapple, **prevent fruit and leaf drop**, maintain **apical dominance**, induce **parthenocarpy** in tomato, control xylem differentiation, and 2,4-D is a **weed killer** for dicots.

questions.solution_md: Darwin, Went; effects of auxins.

questions.stem_md: Describe the discovery and the physiological effects of gibberellins and of cytokinins.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Gibberellins.** They were discovered from the fungus *Gibberella fujikuroi*, which causes the **foolish seedling** disease of rice. They **elongate stems**, increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems (and the yield), cause **bolting** in beet and cabbage, improve the **shape and size of fruits** such as apple, **delay senescence** so that fruits stay on the trees longer, and **speed up malting**.

**Cytokinins.** Kinetin was isolated from autoclaved herring sperm DNA and **zeatin** from maize kernels and coconut milk. Cytokinins promote **cell division**, help produce new leaves, lateral shoots and adventitious shoots, **overcome apical dominance** and **delay leaf senescence** by mobilising nutrients.

questions.solution_md: Gibberellins and cytokinins.

questions.stem_md: Describe the physiological effects of ethylene and of abscisic acid, and explain how each helps a plant, or a farmer, in a situation you name.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Ethylene** is a **gas** formed in ripening fruits and senescing tissues. It **hastens fruit ripening** (tomato, apple), **senescence and abscission** of leaves and flowers, promotes **female flowers** in cucumber, breaks **dormancy** in potato tubers, and promotes **flowering** in pineapple and mango. A farmer uses **ethephon**, which releases ethylene, to ripen fruit evenly.

**Abscisic acid** is the **stress hormone**. It **closes stomata** and raises tolerance to stress, so a plant in drought loses less water; it induces **seed dormancy**, inhibits **germination**, promotes abscission and senescence, and is an **antagonist** of gibberellins.

questions.solution_md: Ethylene and ABA effects with applications.

questions.stem_md: Four coleoptiles are lit from one side: A has an opaque cap over its tip, B has its tip cut off, C has an opaque sheath over its base with the tip uncovered, and D is intact. Predict which will bend towards the light, explain each result, and say what the set shows.

answer.model_answer_md:
**A** (cap on tip) does **not bend**: the tip cannot perceive the light. **B** (tip cut off) does **not bend**: the source of the signal is gone. **C** (sheath over the base, tip exposed) **bends towards the light**: the tip perceives the light and a signal moves down past the sheath. **D** (intact) **bends** towards the light.

**What it shows.** The **tip perceives light** and produces a substance, later shown by Went to be **auxin**, which moves down and causes the cells on the **shaded side** to elongate more, so the coleoptile bends towards the light.

questions.solution_md: Predictions with reasons; conclusion.

marking_scheme.step: A and B do not bend, with reasons
C and D bend, with reasons
Tip perceives; auxin; shaded side grows more

questions.stem_md: A farmer says: “Ethylene is a liquid that stops fruits from ripening, abscisic acid helps seeds to germinate, 2,4-D is good for killing wheat weeds like grasses, and removing the top bud of a tea plant makes it taller.” Evaluate each claim, correct any errors, and say whether any part is right.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Ethylene** is wrong twice: it is a **gas** and it **hastens** ripening. **Abscisic acid** does the opposite of the claim: it **inhibits germination** and induces dormancy; it is the antagonist of gibberellins. **2,4-D** is a synthetic auxin that kills **dicot** weeds, not grasses, which are monocots like wheat, so the claim is wrong. **Removing the top bud** removes apical dominance, so lateral buds grow and the plant becomes **bushier**, not taller.

**Judgement.** Every claim is wrong; the farmer has reversed the effects, so none is correct.

questions.solution_md: Evaluates four claims; all wrong.
